specAnchors.text: use the relationship between final speed, initial speed, acceleration and distance moved: (final speed)2 = (initial speed)2 + (2 × acceleration × distance moved) v2 = u2 + (2 × a × s)

primer.text: One equation of this topic refuses the formula triangle: v² = u² + 2as links four quantities and leaves time out entirely. This lesson states the relationship for uniform acceleration, maps every symbol to its unit, and then practises the plain-algebra rearranging that replaces the triangle.

modules.title: The v² = u² + 2as relationship
modules.opening: Some journeys never tell you their duration — only the speeds at the ends and the acceleration between them. For those, the squared relationship steps in: it connects initial speed, final speed, acceleration and distance moved without ever mentioning time. This lesson pins the equation and the meaning of every letter in it.
keyPoints: Uniform acceleration means constant acceleration: the velocity changes by the same amount every second.
The relationship for uniform acceleration is v² = u² + 2as; each symbol carries a meaning: v the final speed, u the initial speed, a the acceleration and s the distance moved.
The symbols carry s = distance moved in metres, u and v = initial and final speed in m/s, and a = acceleration in m/s².
This equation is the tool when the time taken is not known and is not asked for; it is also the one relationship no cover-and-read triangle can encode.

low.restatement: Square the finishing speed; it equals the square of the starting speed plus two times the acceleration times the distance covered. Use it whenever time never enters the question.
low.analogy: It is a four-piece jigsaw: name any three pieces (two speeds, the acceleration, or the distance) and the equation hands you the fourth.
low.examPointer: Start every answer by listing the known quantities with their symbols; a labelled list earns credit and points straight at the right equation.

medium.restatement: The squares are the price of excluding time: v² = u² + 2as is the time-free combination of the velocity-change relationship with the distance covered under constant acceleration.
medium.analogy: Where a = Δv/t needs a clock, this equation is the shortcut that survives with only the speedometer and the odometer.
medium.examPointer: Watch 'from rest': it pins u = 0 and quietly removes one term from the squares before any arithmetic starts.

modules.title: Rearranging without a triangle
modules.opening: With the triangle unavailable, rearranging falls back on two universal algebra rules: treat both sides identically, and undo operations in reverse. This lesson applies them to isolate s, then runs the full worked car calculation — from rest, at 2.5 m/s², up to 16 m/s — and reads the distance off the end.
keyPoints: Anything done to the equation must be done to both sides, and each operation is undone by its opposite.
To isolate s: subtract u² from both sides, then divide both sides by 2a, giving s = (v² − u²) / (2a).
Squaring is undone by square-rooting, multiplication by division, subtraction by addition.
Showing the rearrangement earns method marks; the worked case gives s = (16² − 0²) / (2 × 2.5) = 256 / 5 = 51.2 m, quoted as 51 m to two significant figures.
Solving for the acceleration works the same when an object uniformly slows: a = (v² − u²) / (2s) comes out negative, and that negative is the deceleration.

low.restatement: To find the distance, first peel the u² off with subtraction, then peel the 2a off with division. What remains on the other side is the answer: v² minus u², all over 2a.
low.analogy: Undoing an equation is like unwrapping a parcel: remove the outermost layer (the division by 2a) last, and the same cut must go through every layer at once.
low.examPointer: Write the rearranged line (s = (v² − u²)/(2a)) before substituting numbers; that single line is usually a method mark.

medium.restatement: The rearrangement order mirrors the equation's construction: 2as was added to u², so subtract u² first; s is multiplied by 2a, so divide last. Each inverse lands on both sides simultaneously.
medium.analogy: Algebraic undressing follows the reverse of dressing: last on, first off, applied everywhere at once.
medium.examPointer: Keep the subtraction order v² − u²; flipping it to u² − v² flips the sign of the whole numerator and, with it, the physics.

glossary.definition: Constant acceleration: the velocity changes by the same amount every second.
The time-free relationship linking final speed, initial speed, acceleration and distance moved under uniform acceleration.
Starting with zero speed; it fixes u = 0 and removes the u² term from the equation.
Rewriting an equation with a different subject by applying the same operation to both sides.

workedExample.prompt: A car accelerates steadily from rest at a rate of 2.5 m/s² up to a speed of 16 m/s. Calculate how far the car moves during this period of acceleration.
steps: List the known quantities: initial speed u = 0 m/s because the car starts from rest; final speed v = 16 m/s; acceleration a = 2.5 m/s².
The phrase 'accelerates steadily' means uniform acceleration, so v² = u² + 2as applies.
Rearrange for distance: subtract u² from both sides, then divide by 2a, giving s = (v² − u²) / (2a).
Substitute: s = (16² − 0²) / (2 × 2.5) = 256 / 5 = 51.2 m, which rounds to 51 m (2 s.f.).
workedExample.finalAnswer: 51.2 m, i.e. 51 m to two significant figures
